brief: Given a newspaper string t and a message s, cut letters from t (each usable once) to spell s. An exact-case match scores YAY; a letter of the right letter but wrong case scores WHOOPS. Maximize YAYs first, then WHOOPSes.
key_idea: Count letters of t; first take all exact-case matches, then pair leftover letters of s with the opposite-case letter still available in t.
solution: Count occurrences of each character of t in a 256-entry array.
Pass 1: for each s[i], if its exact character still has count > 0, use it: yay++, decrement, mark i used.
Pass 2: for each unused s[i], look up its case-flipped letter; if its count > 0, whoops++ and decrement.
Greedy is safe: an exact match is never worse than a case-flipped match, so taking exact matches first cannot lower the YAY count.
Edge case: non-letters have no case flip, so they never add WHOOPS.
complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time, O(1) space (fixed 256-entry array)
dry_run: Sample 3: s = abacaba, t = AbaCaBA; counts of t: A=2, a=2, b=1, B=1, C=1.
Pass 1 (exact): s[0]=a, s[1]=b, s[2]=a use up a=2 and b=1 -> yay = 3; a and b counts are now 0, A=2 remains.
Pass 2 (flip) over unused s[3..6] = c a b a: C -> yes (whoops 1), A -> yes (2), B -> yes (3), A -> yes (4).
Output 3 4, matching the expected output.

brief: Given strings S and T, an abbreviation is interesting if it can be split into a non-empty prefix of S and a non-empty suffix of T in at least two different ways. Output a shortest interesting abbreviation, or -1.
key_idea: Two splits always reduce to one: the last character of S's prefix equals the character just before T's suffix. So the answer is min over letters c of (smallest i2 >= 2 with S[i2-1]=c) + (smallest k >= 1 with T[m-k-1]=c).
solution: Let the abbreviation be S[0..i2) + suffix of T of length k. Take the second split at i2 and the first split at i2-1; both are valid iff S[i2-1] == T[m-k-1] and i2 >= 2, k <= m-1.
Any interesting abbreviation has two splits; the one with the larger S-prefix length gives the same character condition, so the condition is also necessary.
For each letter c, compute bi[c] = smallest i2 in [2, |S|] with S[i2-1] = c, and bk[c] = smallest k in [1, |T|-1] with T[|T|-k-1] = c.
Answer length = min over c with both defined of bi[c] + bk[c]; if none, print -1.
Output S.substr(0, bi[c]) + T.substr(|T| - bk[c]).
complexity: O(|S| + |T|) time, O(1) extra space (26-letter arrays)
dry_run: Sample 1: S = sarana, T = olahraga (m = 8).
bi[a] = 2 (S[1] = a); bk[a] = 2 (T[5] = a); total 4. Other letters give totals >= 5.
Output = S[0..2) + T suffix of length 2 = sa + ga = saga, which matches the expected output.
Check: saga = s + aga (s prefix of S, aga suffix of T) and sa + ga, so two splits exist.

brief: Given a positive integer a (up to 10^18) and at most k adjacent-digit swaps, make the largest possible number.
key_idea: Greedily fix positions left to right: at each position bring the largest digit reachable within the remaining swap budget, choosing the nearest one on ties.
solution: Read the digits as a string s and the budget k.
For position i, look at digits j in [i, i+k] (not past the end) and find the largest digit; on ties keep the smallest j (cheapest).
Move that digit to position i by shifting s[i..j-1] right by one; this costs j - i swaps.
Subtract the cost from k and continue to the next position while k > 0.
Edge case: k = 0 or equal digits leave the string unchanged; the answer has the same length so string comparison is the same as numeric comparison.
complexity: O(L * min(L, k)) time where L is the number of digits (at most 19), O(L) space
dry_run: Sample 3: s = 1034, k = 2.
Budget is spent, nothing else changes.
Output 3104, matching the expected output.

brief: n fruit trees; tree i has b_i fruits ripening on day a_i and collectible only on day a_i or a_i + 1. At most v fruits per day. Maximize total collected.
key_idea: Simulate days in order; on each day spend the daily capacity first on fruit that expires today (ripened yesterday), then on fruit ripening today.
solution: Keep remaining fruit count b_i for each tree.
For day d from 1 to 3001 (max ripening day 3000, plus one day of slack): capacity = v.
First take from trees with a_i = d - 1 (they expire today), then from trees with a_i = d, each time taking min(capacity, b_i).
Add each taken amount to the answer and reduce both capacity and b_i.
Why greedy works: a tree that expires today must use capacity now or lose it, while a fresh tree can wait one more day.
complexity: O(D * n) time with D = 3001, O(n) space
dry_run: Day 1: cap 3, tree1 (ripe day 1) gives 3, left 2. Total 3.
Day 2: expiring tree1 gives 2 (cap 1 left), then tree2 gives 1 (tree2 left 2). Total 6.
Day 3: expiring tree2 gives 2. Total 8, matching the expected output.

brief: 2n people in a line, forming n couples (each value 1..n appears twice). Find the minimum number of adjacent swaps so that every couple stands next to each other.
key_idea: Fix the couples from left to right: for the leftmost unfixed person, bring their partner next to them by adjacent swaps, which is the unavoidable cost.
solution: Walk i = 0, 2, 4, ... over the array.
Find the partner j > i+1 of a[i] (the other occurrence of the same value).
Add j - (i+1) to the answer and shift a[i+1..j] right by one so the partner lands at i+1.
Continue with the next pair; couples already placed are never disturbed.
Greedy is optimal because each adjacent swap can only reduce the gap of one couple by one, so the gap must be closed anyway.
complexity: O(n^2) time with n <= 100, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 3: a = 3 1 2 3 1 2.
i=0 (3): partner at j=3, cost 2 -> a = 3 3 1 2 1 2.
i=2 (1): partner at j=4, cost 1 -> a = 3 3 1 1 2 2.
i=4 (2): partner already adjacent, cost 0. Total 3, matching the expected output.

brief: Interactive: one of two hidden objects (a directed graph on n vertices with edges x_i -> y_i, or n points (x_i, y_i)) must be identified using at most 2 queries of distance (shortest path length, or Manhattan distance) between indices i and j.
key_idea: If some vertex v does not appear in x, query (v, j): graph returns 0 while points always return at least 1, so one query decides. The case where x is a permutation was not solved, so no full strategy is given.
solution: If some vertex v in 1..n is not in x, it has no outgoing edges in object A, so dist(v, j) = 0 for every j != v.
Object B distances are always at least 1, so a response of 0 means A and a response of at least 1 means B.
This gives a one-query answer in that case.
When x is a permutation (every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge), a two-query strategy is needed; it was not derived here.
complexity: O(n) per test to find an unused vertex (interaction cost dominates)
dry_run: Sample test 1: n=3, x = 2 2 3; vertex 1 is not in x.
Query ? 1 2 -> graph gives 0, so the object is A.
Output ! A, which matches the expected answer in test 1 (sample uses a different query, so the trace is own-reasoning only).

brief: A chest holds N coins; players alternate (Chanek first). A move takes exactly one coin, or takes exactly half when the count is even. Each player maximizes their own coins. Output Chanek's optimal total.
key_idea: Let g(n) be the best total for the player to move. Odd n forces taking 1; for even n the choice is take 1 or take half. A DP check shows: n = 2 mod 4 or n = 4 -> take half; other even n -> take 1. This gives O(log N) recursion.
solution: Define g(0) = 0 and g(n) = max over legal moves of (coins taken + (n - taken) - g(n - taken)).
Take 1: value = 1 + (n-1 - g(n-1)). Take half (n even): value = n/2 + (n/2 - g(n/2)).
Verified by DP up to 3000: for n = 2 mod 4 or n = 4, half is optimal (or tied); for all other even n, take 1 is optimal (or tied).
Implement g recursively: odd n or n = 0 mod 4 (n != 4) -> take 1; otherwise -> half. Recursion depth is O(log N) because each step either halves or goes to n-1 then n-2.
Read T test cases and print g(N) for each; use long long since N <= 10^18.
complexity: O(log N) time per test case, O(log N) stack space
dry_run: Outputs 4 and 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Given n integers, pick 8 of them as the coordinates of an axis-parallel rectangle's four corners (values may be reused only as often as they occur) to maximize area. Print NO if impossible.
key_idea: A rectangle needs four values each used twice, so take the multiset of pairs (value v contributes count/2 pairs), sort it, and test the two ways of splitting the four extreme pairs into x and y sides.
solution: Count occurrences of each value; build list P with floor(count/2) copies of each value, sorted ascending.
If |P| < 4, print NO.
Let m = |P|. Candidate 1: x from (P[0], P[m-2]), y from (P[1], P[m-1]), area (P[m-2]-P[0])*(P[m-1]-P[1]).
Candidate 2: x from (P[0], P[m-1]), y from (P[1], P[m-2]), area (P[m-1]-P[0])*(P[m-2]-P[1]).
Print YES and the 8 corner coordinates (x1,y1),(x1,y2),(x2,y1),(x2,y2) for the better candidate. Verified against brute force on 3000 random small arrays.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test (sorting by map), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: pairs from values 1..7 (each count 2), so P = 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 (m = 7).
Pick candidate 1: x = 1, 6 and y = 2, 7; print 1 2 1 7 6 2 6 7.
Sample 2 has pairs 0,1,2 only (m = 3), so the answer is NO. Output matches the expected output.

brief: n cups with volumes a_i, a teapot with w ml (w <= sum a_i). Each cup must hold at least half its volume (ceil), all tea must be poured, and a cup with a larger volume may not hold less tea than a smaller one. Output amounts or -1.
key_idea: Give every cup its minimum ceil(a_i/2); if the total minimum exceeds w, answer -1. Then pour the leftover into cups in decreasing volume order, filling each to full before moving on.
solution: Set b_i = ceil(a_i / 2) and need = sum b_i. If need > w print -1.
Let r = w - need, the leftover to distribute.
Visit cups in decreasing order of a_i; add t = min(r, a_i - b_i) to b_i and subtract t from r.
Ordering check: if a_i > a_j and j gets extra tea, then i was already full (b_i = a_i > b_j), so the rule holds.
Print b_i in the original input order.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 8 7, w = 10; minimums 4 and 4, need = 8, r = 2.
Largest first: cup a=8 gets t = min(2, 8-4) = 2 -> b = 6, r = 0.
Cup a=7 gets 0 -> b = 4.
Output 6 4, matching the expected output.

brief: n users each need a rating at least a_i. Assign distinct integer ratings b_i >= a_i with minimum total sum. Output b in input order.
key_idea: Sort users by required rating and assign each the smallest value that is at least its requirement and larger than the previous assigned rating.
solution: Sort indices by a_i ascending.
Keep prev = the last assigned rating (initially 0).
For each index in sorted order, set b = max(a_i, prev + 1) and set prev = b.
This is optimal: any valid assignment must have the k-th smallest rating at least the k-th smallest greedy value.
Output b in the original order; use long long since values can reach about 10^9 + 3*10^5.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 5 1 1. Sorted by a: index1 (1), index2 (1), index0 (5).
index1: b = max(1, 0+1) = 1; prev = 1.
index2: b = max(1, 2) = 2; prev = 2.
index0: b = max(5, 3) = 5. Output 5 1 2, matching the expected output.

brief: n people each have a first name and a last name. Each person chooses one of the two as the handle. Given a permutation p, decide whether the handles can be chosen so that h[p_1] < h[p_2] < ... < h[p_n] in lexicographic order.
key_idea: Only consecutive pairs in p are constrained, so the constraints form a chain. A two-state DP over positions in p (choose first or last name) decides feasibility in O(n) string comparisons.
solution: Read names as option 0 (first) and option 1 (last) for each person, and read the permutation p.
Let feas[c] for the current person be true if some valid prefix ends with that person choosing option c; start with both true for p_1.
For each consecutive pair (a, b) = (p_k, p_{k+1}), set nfeas[cb] = true when some feasible ca gives name(a, ca) < name(b, cb).
If both entries become false at any step, print NO; otherwise print YES after the chain ends.
Lexicographic string comparison (std::string <) matches the required order.
complexity: O(n * L) time where L <= 50 is the name length, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: p = 3 1 2, names: person1 (gennady, korotkevich), person2 (petr, mitrichev), person3 (gaoyuan, chen).
Pair (3,1): person3 chen or gaoyuan < person1 gennady or korotkevich -> feasible with gaoyuan or chen (both < gennady).
Pair (1,2): person1 gennady < person2 petr -> feasible; the chain stays feasible, print YES.
Sample 1 (p = 1 2 3): person2 must be above person3's name in the chain, which fails, so NO. Output matches.

brief: Array a of n integers; one move adds 1 to every element of a chosen range [l, r]. Find the minimum number of moves to make the array non-decreasing.
key_idea: Each move raises at most one adjacent difference by 1 (the one at l-1), so the answer is the total descent sum of max(0, a[i] - a[i+1]); a move on [i+1, n] achieves exactly one unit of fix.
solution: Compute the total descent D = sum over i of max(0, a[i] - a[i+1]).
Lower bound: a range +1 move changes a single adjacent difference by +1 (on the left boundary) and only decreases the right boundary's difference, so total descent drops by at most 1 per move.
Upper bound: applying the move on [i+1, n] for each unit of descent at i fixes that descent and does not create new ones.
Print D. Use 64-bit since D can reach about 10^14.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 3: a = 7 4 1 47; descents: 7-4=3, 4-1=3, 1<47 gives 0.
D = 3 + 3 = 6. Output 6, matching the expected output.
Own example: a = 5 2 4; descents: 5-2 = 3, 2<4 gives 0; D = 3, so 3 moves (add 1 to [2,3] three times) make 5 5 5 or similar non-decreasing.

brief: n towers of distinct numbered blocks (listed top to bottom). Operations: split a tower's top part into a new tower, or combine one whole tower onto another. Goal: one tower with blocks sorted (smallest on top). Output the minimum number of splits and combines.
key_idea: An adjacency x-above-y in a starting tower is kept only if y is the next larger block overall. Every other adjacency must be cut by a split, so splits = number of bad adjacencies, and combines = n + splits - 1.
solution: Collect all block values, sort them, so each value's successor in sorted order is known.
For each tower and each adjacent pair (x above y), count it as good if y is the successor of x in the sorted list.
Let N = total blocks, n = number of towers, good = count of good adjacencies. Bad adjacencies = (N - n) - good.
Splits s = bad. Each split adds one tower, and every tower must eventually be combined, so combines c = n + s - 1.
Print s and c. Verified on the sample (1 split, 2 combines); the lower bound follows since each bad adjacency must be separated.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run: Sample: towers (3 5 8) and (9 2); all sorted: 2 3 5 8 9.
Adjacencies: 3-5 (successor of 3 is 5, good), 5-8 (good), 9-2 (bad). Bad = 1.
s = 1, c = 2 + 1 - 1 = 2. Output 1 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Two n x m matrices A and B. You may swap A[i][j] with B[i][j] at any cell. Decide whether both matrices can be made strictly increasing along every row and column.
key_idea: Put the smaller value of every cell into A and the larger into B; this is the only choice that can work, so check both matrices for strict increase.
solution: For every cell (i, j), let lo = min(A, B) and hi = max(A, B).
Set A[i][j] = lo and B[i][j] = hi (swap when needed).
Check every row and column of A and of B for strict increase (compare with right and down neighbours).
Print Possible if both pass, otherwise Impossible.
Why this is optimal: any valid arrangement has A at each cell no larger than the min and B no smaller than the max, so forcing min into A is never worse.
complexity: O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space
dry_run: A = [2 4; 3 5]: rows 2<4 and 3<5, columns 2<3 and 4<5, OK. B = [9 10; 11 12] is also increasing.
Output Possible, matching the expected output.

brief: Camera with d MB. Client i needs x_i low-quality photos (a MB each) and y_i high-quality photos (b MB each), all or nothing. Choose the largest set of clients whose total memory is at most d and print them.
key_idea: Each client has a fixed memory cost x_i*a + y_i*b; to maximize the count, serve the cheapest clients first until the budget runs out.
solution: Compute cost_i = x_i * a + y_i * b for each client (fits in 64-bit: at most about 2*10^9).
Sort clients by cost ascending.
Take clients in that order while the running total plus cost_i stays at most d; stop at the first client that does not fit.
Print the number of chosen clients and their 1-based indices (an empty second line if none).
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a=2, b=3, d=10; costs: client1 = 1*2+4*3 = 14, client2 = 2*2+1*3 = 7, client3 = 1*2+0 = 2.
Sorted: client3 (2), client2 (7), client1 (14). Take 3 (total 2), take 2 (total 9), client1 would reach 23 > 10, stop.
Output 2 then 3 2, matching the expected output.

brief: n knights with distinct powers p_i and coins c_i. A knight can kill any weaker knight (strictly smaller power), up to k kills, taking the victim's coins. For each knight output the maximum coins he can end with.
key_idea: Sort by power. A knight's best kills are the k richest weaker knights, so keep a min-heap of the k largest coin values seen so far among weaker knights and a running sum.
solution: Sort knights by power ascending.
Walk in that order. For knight i, answer = c_i + (sum of the heap), where the heap holds up to k largest coin values of strictly weaker knights.
Then push c_i into the heap and its sum; if the heap has more than k entries, pop the smallest.
If k = 0, the answer is just c_i.
Print answers in the original order.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (heap size <= k <= 10)
dry_run: Sample 1: k = 2; sorted by power: (4, c=1), (5, c=2), (7, c=33), (9, c=11).
Knight 4: heap empty -> 1; push 1. Knight 5: 2 + 1 = 3; push 2 (heap {1, 2}, sum 3).
Knight 7: 33 + 3 = 36; push 33, pop 1 (heap {2, 33}, sum 35). Knight 9: 11 + 35 = 46.
Output 1 3 46 36 in input order, matching the expected output.

brief: Given 4^k integers (count is a power of 4), place them in a 2^k x 2^k matrix to maximize beauty, where beauty = max of the whole matrix + the beauties of its four quadrants, recursively.
key_idea: Each value's weight is the number of recursion levels where it is a block maximum. Sort descending and give the largest value weight k+1, the next 3 weight k, the next 12 weight k-1, and so on.
solution: Let the count be 4^k and sort the values in descending order.
Level 0 has one block (the whole matrix): its max, the largest value, is counted at levels 0..k, so it gets weight k+1.
Level j (1 <= j <= k) introduces 3 * 4^(j-1) new block maxima, each counted at levels j..k, so weight k + 1 - j.
Sum value * weight over all values in sorted order using this schedule.
Placement that achieves this: put each new maximum in the quadrant structure so the largest values sit at the top of the recursion.
complexity: O(N log N) time for N = 4^k values (sorting dominates), O(N) space
dry_run: Sample 2: count 4, so k = 1. Sorted desc: 4, 3, 2, 1.
Largest value 4 gets weight k+1 = 2 -> 8.
Next 3 values (3, 2, 1) get weight k+1-1 = 1 -> 6.
Total 14, matching the expected output (4 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4).

brief: n engineers must finish k units of work. Engineer i gets bonus a_i only if the total reaches k, and each unit costs b_i. Engineers decide in order 1..n, each maximizing own benefit; output each engineer's work.
key_idea: Each engineer's maximum non-negative work is cap_i = a_i / b_i. Engineer i does only the least amount that later engineers cannot cover: c_i = max(0, R - (sum of later caps)), where R is the work still needed. If total caps < k, nobody works.
solution: Compute cap_i = a_i / b_i (integer division) and the suffix sums suf[i] = cap_i + ... + cap_{n-1}.
If suf[0] < k, print all zeros.
Otherwise walk i = 0..n-1 with R = remaining work (initially k): set c_i = max(0, R - suf[i+1]).
Subtract c_i from R and move on. Invariant: R <= suf[i] holds, so c_i <= cap_i and the benefit a_i - c_i*b_i is never negative.
Check with sample 3: caps 6, 3, 2 give c = 6, 3, 2.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Output 1 3 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Buy n items with m discount types (basket size q_i). With a discount, after filling a basket of q_i paid items you may take up to two free items, each no pricier than the cheapest item in that basket. Minimize total payment.
key_idea: The smallest q (qmin) is always the best basket size. Sort prices descending and group them in blocks of qmin+2; the two cheapest items of each block are free.
solution: Let qmin = minimum of all q_i; discounts can be reused, so the smallest basket is best.
Sort the prices in descending order.
Within each block of qmin + 2 consecutive items (starting at the most expensive), the first qmin are paid and the last two are free.
Free items are cheaper than or equal to the basket's cheapest item, so each block is valid.
Sum the paid items; this is the minimum because pricier items should be the paid basket.
complexity: O(n log n) time (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: qmin = 2, sorted desc: 100 100 50 50; block size 4 covers all four, indices 2 and 3 are free.
Paid: 100 + 100 = 200. Output 200, matching the expected output.
Sample 2: qmin = 2, five 50s; blocks of 4: indices 0,1 paid, 2,3 free, index 4 paid (i%4 = 0).
Paid = 3 * 50 = 150, matching the expected output.

brief: Find n positive integers whose sum is at most y and whose sum of squares is at least x, or print -1.
key_idea: For a fixed sum, the sum of squares is maximized by concentrating it in one element. Use one element y - (n-1) and n-1 ones; this is feasible iff y >= n and (y-n+1)^2 + (n-1) >= x.
solution: If y < n, no n positive integers fit: print -1.
Let big = y - (n - 1) and check big^2 + (n - 1) >= x; if not, print -1 (no other choice gives more squares with this sum).
Otherwise print big and then n-1 ones (sum = y, squares >= x).
Use 64-bit arithmetic: big^2 can be about 10^12.
complexity: O(n) time for output, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Output 11 1 1 1 1 (sum 15, squares 125). Any valid answer is accepted, so this is fine.
Sample 2: n=2, x=3, y=2. y >= n holds, big = 1, squares = 1 + 1 = 2 < 3, so -1.

brief: For each n, build an array with elements in [0, n] that maximizes beauty = length minus the number of zero-XOR subarrays, and among optimal arrays the longest one. Print its length and elements.
key_idea: Prefix XORs form a walk on values below 2^L (L = bit length of n) where consecutive values differ by an element <= n. Beauty = sum over values of (count - C(count,2)) - 1, maximized at 2^L - 1 by visiting every value exactly twice, which a Gray code walk followed by its reverse achieves.
solution: Let L be the smallest value with 2^L > n and N = 2^L. Prefix XORs stay in [0, N), so at most N distinct prefix values count.
Each value visited once or twice contributes exactly 1 to beauty; more visits lower it. So beauty <= N - 1, and visiting every value exactly twice gives length 2N - 1 (longest).
Build seq = Gray code G_0..G_{N-1} (G_i = i xor (i >> 1)), followed by G_{N-1}..G_0.
Output k = 2N - 1 and a_j = seq[j-1] xor seq[j] for j = 1..k. Gray steps are single powers of two <= 2^(L-1) <= n, and the middle step is 0, both allowed.
Verified in Python for n = 1..129: beauty = N - 1 and length = 2N - 1.
complexity: O(N) time per test to output 2N - 1 numbers where N = 2^L (about 2n), O(N) space
dry_run: n = 1: L = 1, N = 2. Gray code: 0, 1. seq = 0 1 1 0.
Prefix XORs: 0 1 1 0, so counts are 2 and 2, beauty = 3 - 1 - 1 = 1 = N - 1.

brief: A full binary tree of depth n (roads numbered 2..2^(n+1)-1, each with a_i lights). Add lights to roads so that every root-to-leaf path has the same total. Minimize the number of lights added.
key_idea: Work bottom-up. At each internal node, the two child subtrees have path totals t1 and t2; add |t1 - t2| lights to the smaller side and pass max(t1, t2) up.
solution: Let f[v] = lights on every path from v down to a leaf (f = 0 at leaves), equal for all paths after balancing.
For node v with children c1, c2, set t1 = f[c1] + a[c1] and t2 = f[c2] + a[c2] (road to child included).
Add |t1 - t2| to the answer (lights added on the cheaper branch).
Set f[v] = max(t1, t2) and continue up to the root.
Greedy is optimal: raising the lower side to the max is forced and never hurts the levels above.
complexity: O(2^n) time, O(2^n) space (n <= 10, at most 2047 nodes)
dry_run: Node 2: children 4, 5 give t = 3 and 4, add 1, f[2] = 4.
Node 3: children 6, 7 give t = 5 and 6, add 1, f[3] = 6.
Root 1: children 2, 3 give t = f[2] + a2 = 5 and f[3] + a3 = 8, add 3. Total 1 + 1 + 3 = 5, matching the expected output.

brief: n threads sorted by latest message. Posting a message moves a thread to the top. After a refresh, the thread at position i was at position a_i before. Count threads that surely received a new message.
key_idea: Threads without a new message keep their old relative order and sit at the bottom, so the untouched ones form the longest increasing run at the end of a. Everything above that run surely got a message.
solution: Scan from the end while a[i-1] < a[i] to find the start i of the longest increasing suffix of a.
Threads in that suffix could all be untouched (they keep their old relative order at the bottom).
Any thread at a position before i cannot be untouched: it would have to sit below a thread with a smaller old position.
Answer = i (0-indexed start of the increasing suffix, equal to the count of positions before it).
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 5 2 1 3 4. From the end: 3 < 4 keeps i at 3; 1 < 3 moves i to 2; 2 < 1 is false, stop.
Answer = i = 2, matching the expected output.
Sample 3: a = 4 3 2 1; no increasing pair at the end, so i = 3 and the answer is 3, matching the expected output.

brief: A string of '+' (someone enters) and '-' (someone leaves) events for a club. People may already be inside at the start. Find the minimum number of distinct people that can explain the log.
key_idea: Each person's events must alternate in sign, so the log is split into alternating subsequences. Greedily attach each event to a chain that ends with the opposite sign, and start a new person only when none exists.
solution: Track endPlus = number of people whose last event was '+' and endMinus = number whose last event was '-'.
On '+': if endMinus > 0, one such person enters now (endMinus--); otherwise a new person is needed (count++). Then endPlus++.
On '-': if endPlus > 0, one such person leaves now (endPlus--); otherwise a new person (already inside at the start) is needed (count++). Then endMinus++.
Any chain ending in the opposite sign works, so the greedy choice does not matter; the count of new persons is minimal.
Output the count.
complexity: O(L) time, O(1) space (L <= 300)
dry_run: Sample 2: '---'. First '-': endPlus = 0, so new person (count 1), endMinus = 1.
Second '-': endPlus = 0, new person (count 2), endMinus = 2. Third '-': new person (count 3).
Output 3, matching the expected output. For '+-+-+' the first '+' starts one person and every later event reuses them, output 1.

brief: N astronauts with current scores S (sorted descending) and a race prize list P (sorted descending). Each astronaut gets one prize. For astronaut at current position D, find the best final rank (ties share the best rank).
key_idea: Give astronaut D the largest prize (an exchange argument shows this never hurts). Then maximize the number of other astronauts whose new total is at most D's total, using a two-pointer greedy on sorted scores and prizes.
solution: Let T = S[D] + P[1] (D takes the largest prize).
Collect the other astronauts' scores (ascending) and the remaining prizes P[2..N] (ascending).

Two pointers: i over scores from the weakest, j over prizes from the largest. If score[i] + prize[j] <= T, count a good pair and advance both; otherwise drop prize[j] (too big for even the weakest score).
Let good be the count of pairs. Astronauts above D = (N - 1) - good, so the best rank = N - good.
Verified against brute force over all prize assignments for 400 random small cases.
complexity: O(N log N) time, O(N) space
dry_run: Others sorted: scores 10, 30, 50; prizes 3, 7, 10.
Rank = N - good = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Soup needs a_i * x litres of ingredient i (x >= 0) from b_i litres available, in a pan of capacity V. Find the largest soup volume (a real number).
key_idea: The soup volume is x * sum(a_i) where x is limited by the scarcest ingredient, x = min(b_i / a_i). Cap the result at V.
solution: Compute x = min over i of b_i / a_i (as a real number).
Compute the total of a_i; the volume at that x is x * sum(a).
The answer is min(V, x * sum(a)).
Print with enough decimals (the checker allows error 1e-4).
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Volume = 25 * 2 = 50, below V.
Output 50.000000, matching the expected 50.0.

brief: Given a target string s and sheet length n, choose a length-n sticker design so that the minimum number of sheets (each with that design) can supply the letters of s. Print the minimum count and a design, or -1.
key_idea: For k sheets, each letter c needs ceil(need_c / k) copies on one sheet, and these must fit within n. Try k = 1, 2, ... and take the first k whose total fits; pad the design with any letter.
solution: Count need[c] for each letter in s.
For k from 1 to |s|: compute total = sum over letters with need > 0 of ceil(need / k).
The first k with total <= n is the answer; the design has ceil(need_c / k) copies of each needed letter plus n - total filler letters.
If no k works (for example when distinct letters exceed n), print -1.
Each needed letter appears on every sheet at least once, so every letter in s is reachable.
complexity: O(|s| * 26) time, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 2: s = banana (a=3, b=1, n=2), n = 3.
Output 3 and design abn (one each). Sample 3 has three distinct letters with n = 2, so no k works and the output is -1.

brief: Given n integers in [-100, 100], choose a non-empty subset whose product is maximum, and print its elements.
key_idea: Take all nonzero numbers if the count of negatives is even; if odd, drop the negative closest to zero. Zero or a single negative needs a special case.
solution: Separate zeros, negatives and positives (nonzero values). If there are no nonzero values, answer 0.
If the number of negatives is even, print all nonzero values (product positive).
If odd and at least two nonzero values exist, drop the negative with the largest value (closest to zero); the rest has a positive product.
If odd and only one nonzero value (a negative): print 0 if a zero exists, else print that single value.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: costs 1 2 -3 3 3. The nonzero negatives are {-3}, an odd count, so drop -3.
Remaining 1 2 3 3 with product 18. The expected output 3 1 2 3 is the same multiset, so this matches.
Sample 3: four -2s, even count, print all: product 16.

brief: Company R2 plays Jeopardy. There are n questions, m of them auctions with base prices. R2 answers everything correctly and picks each next question. An auction can be raised to R2's current points if points are strictly greater than the base price. Maximize R2's final score.
key_idea: Take all regular questions first, then the auctions in descending order of price. An auction with price < current points doubles the score (raise to all points); otherwise add its price. If there are no regular questions, the first pick is the largest auction.
solution: Split questions into regular (sum R) and auction prices; sort auctions in descending order.
Start with S = R (regular questions can't be raised, so take them first to grow S before doublings).
If there are no regular questions, the first pick cannot be raised (S = 0): set S = largest auction and drop it from the list.
For each remaining auction p in descending order: if S > p then S = 2S (raise to S), else S = S + p.
Checked against brute force over all pick orders for 3000 random instances with n <= 6.
complexity: O(m log m) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: regular 1 3 5 sum to 9; auction 7. 9 > 7, so S = 18.
Sample 2: regular 10; auctions 8 then 3 (descending). 10 > 8 gives 20; 20 > 3 gives 40.
Sample 3: no regular. First pick 200 (S = 200); auction 100: 200 > 100 gives 400, matching the expected output.

brief: A chronological log of messages (sender, receiver, time) with a response window d. Two users are friends if one answered the other's message: a reply at time t2 to a message at time t1 with 0 < t2 - t1 <= d. List all friend pairs once.
key_idea: For each message i, scan later messages j for a reply from the receiver back to the sender with 0 < t_j - t_i <= d; store each unordered pair in a set. n <= 1000 makes the O(n^2) scan fine.
solution: Read the messages in order (sender, receiver, time).
For each pair i < j, check that j goes back (from = to[i], to = from[i]) and 0 < t[j] - t[i] <= d.
If so, insert the unordered pair (sorted names) into a set so each pair appears once.
Print the set size and then the pairs.
Same-time messages are excluded by the strict t_j - t_i > 0 check.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (n <= 1000)
dry_run: Sample 1: message 1 vasya->petya at t=1; message 2 petya->vasya at t=2: difference 1 <= d=1, so the pair (petya, vasya) is added.
Message 3 anya->ivan at t=2 and message 4 ivan->anya at t=4: difference 2 > 1, not friends.
Output 1 then petya vasya, matching the expected output.

brief: Given a name s and a string t, count the cut positions of t such that the left part and the right part each contain s as a (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence.
key_idea: Find the shortest prefix of t containing s as a subsequence (greedy scan from the left, length lo) and the latest start of a suffix containing s (greedy scan from the right, index hi). Valid cuts are lo <= cut <= hi, so the count is hi - lo + 1.
solution: Scan t from left, matching s greedily; when all of s is matched at index i, set lo = i + 1 (shortest valid left part).
Scan t from right, matching s from its end; when all of s is matched at index i, set hi = i (latest valid start of the right part).
If either scan fails, or hi < lo, print 0.
Otherwise the cut positions lo, lo+1, ..., hi are all valid, so print hi - lo + 1.
Greedy matching is optimal for subsequence checks, which gives the exact boundaries.
complexity: O(|t| + |s|) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 1: s = aba, t = b a o b a b a b b a h. Left greedy matches a(1), b(3), a(4): lo = 5.
Right greedy from the end matches a(9), b(8), a(6): hi = 6.
Count = 6 - 5 + 1 = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Stations at increasing positions x_1 < ... < x_n from school (x_1) to home (x_n). A bike can be ridden at most k km before it must be returned at a station, and only one bike can be held at a time. Find the minimum number of bikes, or -1 if impossible.
key_idea: Each bike ride goes from the current station to the farthest station within k km. Jumping as far as possible each time is optimal; if the next station is already out of reach, the answer is -1.
solution: Start at station 0 with count = 0.
While not at the last station: find the farthest index j > pos with x[j] - x[pos] <= k.
If no such j exists (the next station is too far), print -1.
Otherwise move to j and increase count by 1 (one bike used).
Print count when home is reached. The farthest-first jump is a classic greedy with an exchange argument.
complexity: O(n^2) time in this direct scan (n <= 1000), O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 1: x = 3 6 8 10, k = 4. From 3, reachable up to 7, so the farthest is 6 (count 1).
From 6, reachable up to 10, so the farthest is 10 (count 2), which is home. Output 2.
Sample 2: x = 10 20, k = 9: from 10 the next station 20 is 10 km away, so -1.

brief: Two adjacent towers start at heights a and b and must reach c and d (a <= c, b <= d). One action adds a block to one tower, or adds one block to both when their heights are equal. Find the minimum number of actions.
key_idea: Let x = c - a, y = d - b and D0 = b - a. The number of joint moves t is maximized subject to having enough single moves to equalize first: t = min(x - D0, y) if D0 >= 0, else t = min(x, y + D0), clamped at 0. Answer = x + y - t.
solution: Compute x = c - a, y = d - b, and D0 = b - a (height difference at the start).
Joint moves only happen when heights are equal, and they keep the difference unchanged, so they are as many as possible.
If D0 >= 0, tower 1 must take D0 single moves to equalize, so t = min(x - D0, y); if D0 < 0, tower 2 must take -D0 moves, so t = min(x, y + D0).
Clamp t at 0 (no joint moves possible), then the answer is x + y - t.
Verified against BFS over all move sequences on 729 small cases.
complexity: O(1) per test case, O(t) total
dry_run: Answer = 2 + 3 - 1 = 4, matching the expected output.
Sample 4: a=3, b=3, c=6, d=4: x = 3, y = 1, D0 = 0, t = min(3, 1) = 1, answer = 3, matching the expected output.

brief: A boot camp of n days; excursion days (0) have no lectures, other days (1) have at most k1 lectures, and any two consecutive days together have at most k2 lectures. Maximize the total number of lectures.
key_idea: Inside each run of regular days, fill greedily from the left: each day gets min(k1, k2 - previous day), or k1 at the start of a run. Excursion days break the chain.
solution: Walk the days, keeping prev = lectures on the previous day if it was a regular day (or none after an excursion or at the start).
On an excursion day, output 0 and reset prev.
On a regular day, take x = k1 if there is no previous day in the run, otherwise x = min(k1, k2 - prev).
Add x to the total and set prev = x.
Greedy is optimal for this path constraint (checked by a DP over all values on 400 random small cases).
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=4, k1=5, k2=7, s=1011. Day 1 (regular, no previous): 5. Day 2 (excursion): 0, reset.
Day 3 (regular, no previous): 5. Day 4 (regular, prev=5): min(5, 7 - 5) = 2.
Total 12, matching the expected output.

brief: Array a of n values and q range queries [l, r]. Before answering, the array may be reordered arbitrarily. Maximize the sum of all query answers.
key_idea: Count how many queries cover each index using a difference array, then pair the largest values with the largest counts (rearrangement inequality).
solution: Build diff: for each query, diff[l] += 1 and diff[r+1] -= 1.
Prefix-sum diff to get freq[i] = number of queries covering index i.
Sort freq in descending order and the array values in descending order.
Answer = sum of freq[i] * a[i] over the sorted lists; this is maximal by the rearrangement inequality.
Use 64-bit sums: values and counts can each be about 2*10^5.
complexity: O((n + q) + n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 5 3 2; queries [1,2], [2,3], [1,3]. Frequencies: index1 = 2, index2 = 3, index3 = 2.
Sorted freq 3, 2, 2 with sorted values 5, 3, 2: 15 + 6 + 4 = 25, matching the expected output.

brief: Array a. In second x you may add 2^(x-1) to any set of distinct elements. Find the minimum number of seconds T so that the array becomes non-decreasing.
key_idea: Each element can receive any integer in [0, 2^T - 1] in total. Greedily keep the running maximum; the largest deficit D = max(prefix max - a_i) must satisfy 2^T - 1 >= D, so T = smallest value with 2^T > D.
solution: Track pref = running maximum of a, and D = max over i of (pref - a_i).
Element i needs at least pref_i - a_i extra; giving exactly that is the smallest feasible value and keeps the array non-decreasing.
Any extra in [0, 2^T - 1] can be built from bits of the seconds, so the condition is D <= 2^T - 1.
Find the smallest T with 2^T >= D + 1 and print it (0 when D = 0).
Use 64-bit integers since a_i can be about 10^9 in magnitude.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 1 7 6 5. pref = 1, 7, 7, 7; deficits 0, 0, 1, 2; D = 2.
Smallest T with 2^T >= 3 is T = 2, matching the expected output.
Sample 3: a = 0 -4; deficit at index 2 is 0 - (-4) = 4, so D = 4 and 2^T >= 5 gives T = 3, matching.

brief: Array of n positive integers. An operation chooses two different positions and decreases each of them by 1. Decide whether all elements can be made zero.
key_idea: Each operation removes 2 units from the total, so the sum must be even; and the largest element can be paired with at most the sum of the others, so max <= sum - max is required. These two conditions are sufficient.
solution: Compute sum and the maximum element mx.
If sum is odd, print NO (each operation removes exactly 2 units).
If mx > sum - mx, print NO (the largest element cannot be reduced without pairing with others).
Otherwise print YES; the two conditions suffice, verified by BFS over all operation sequences on 300 random small arrays.
complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample 1: 1 1 2 2. sum = 6 (even), mx = 2 <= 4 = sum - mx, so YES.
Sample 2: 1 2 3 4 5 6. sum = 21 is odd, so NO, matching the expected output.

brief: n hordes of monsters with sizes a_i. Attack type 1 kills one monster in a horde and raises the combo x by 1; attack type 2 kills x monsters from a horde holding at least x and resets x to 0. Find the minimum number of attacks to clear all hordes.
key_idea: A type-2 phase after x type-1 kills saves x - 1 attacks and needs x monsters for itself, so at most floor(S/2) monsters can be used by type-2 phases. Using the k largest hordes gives savings min(floor(S/2), prefix_k) - k; take the best k.
solution: Let S = total monsters and B = floor(S/2), the most monsters that type-2 attacks can absorb (each phase needs as many type-1 kills).
Sort hordes in descending order and let pref_k be the sum of the k largest.
For each k >= 1, savings_k = min(B, pref_k) - k (one type-2 phase per chosen horde saves its combo minus one).
Answer = S - max(0, max over k of savings_k).
Checked on all samples and against BFS over all attack sequences for 150 small cases.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test case (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 4: hordes 1 and 6, so S = 7 and B = 3. Sorted: 6, 1.
k = 1: pref = 6, min(3, 6) - 1 = 2. k = 2: min(3, 7) - 2 = 1. Best savings = 2.
Answer = 7 - 2 = 5, matching the expected output (kill 1 with type 1, then 3 type 1 on the 6-horde, one type 2 of 3, then 1 type 1).

brief: A word of length n is k-complete if it is a palindrome with period k (n divisible by k). Given a lowercase word s, find the minimum number of letter replacements that turn it into a k-complete word.
key_idea: Positions with the same residue mod k must match, and residues r and k-1-r must match (palindrome). Group those residues, and in each group keep the most frequent letter; the cost is group size minus that frequency.
solution: Let blocks = n / k. Count letter frequencies cnt[r][c] for each residue r in [0, k).
For each residue r with partner p = k - 1 - r and r <= p: merge the counts of r and p (if p != r).
Group size is 2 * blocks for a pair of different residues, or blocks when r = p.
Cost for the group is group size minus the largest letter count.
Sum the costs over all groups. Checked against brute force for 200 small cases.
complexity: O(n + 26k) time per test case, O(26k) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=6, k=2, s = abaaba. Residue 0 holds positions 0, 2, 4 = a, a, b; residue 1 holds 1, 3, 5 = b, a, a.
Partner of 0 is 1 (k-1-0 = 1), so the group has 6 positions with a = 4, b = 2.
Cost = 6 - 4 = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Find a shortest lowercase string containing at least k subsequences equal to 'codeforces'.
key_idea: Use ten blocks, one per letter of 'codeforces', with x_i copies of the i-th letter. The number of subsequences is the product of the x_i, so keep the x_i balanced: increase them round-robin until the product reaches k.
solution: Start with x_i = 1 for all ten positions of 'codeforces'.
While the product of the x_i is less than k, increment the next x_i in cyclic order.
The product stays below 2k, so 64-bit integers are safe.
Output each letter of 'codeforces' repeated x_i times, in order.
Balanced counts minimize the sum for a fixed product, so the length is minimal.
complexity: O(10 * log k) time, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample k = 3: all x = 1 (product 1 < 3). Increment x_0 (product 2), then x_1 (product 4 >= 3).
String: cc oo deforces = ccoodeforces, length 12 with 4 subsequences. The expected output has the same length and is also valid.
Sample k = 1: product is already 1, so the output is codeforces.

brief: Given n and s, find the minimum number of increments that makes the digit sum of n at most s.
key_idea: If the digit sum is already small, answer 0. Otherwise find the smallest m' > n with digit sum <= s: keep the longest common prefix with n, raise the first differing digit, and zero the lower digits (zeros are free).
solution: If digitsum(n) <= s, print 0.
For position p = 0, 1, 2, ... (from the lowest digit): let dig = digit p of n and high = n / 10^(p+1).
If dig < 9 and digitsum(high) + dig + 1 <= s, the candidate is n' = (high * 10 + dig + 1) * 10^p; the first such p gives the smallest candidate.
Print n' - n.
Verified against brute force on 300 random cases with n up to 3000.
complexity: O(18 * 18) time per test case, O(1) space
dry_run: Sample: n = 2, s = 1. Digit sum 2 > 1. p = 0: dig = 2, digit sum 0 + 3 > 1, fail.
Output 10 - 2 = 8, matching the expected output.

brief: Connected undirected graph (multi-edges and self-loops allowed) with n nodes. Bob starts at node 1 and records each node the first time he reaches it. Output the lexicographically smallest recorded order.
key_idea: Grow the visited set like Prim: keep a min-heap of frontier vertices (neighbours of visited ones) and always visit the smallest unvisited frontier vertex next.
solution: Build adjacency lists; mark node 1 visited, record it, and push all its neighbours into a min-heap.
Pop the smallest vertex; skip it if already visited (duplicates are allowed in the heap).
Otherwise mark it visited, append it to the order, and push its unvisited neighbours.
Repeat until the heap is empty; the recorded order is the answer.
Greedy is right because the next recorded vertex must be some frontier vertex, and the smallest one is always the best lexicographically.
complexity: O((n + m) log m) time, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 2: edges 1-4, 3-4, 5-4, 3-2, 1-5. Start at 1; heap {4, 5}. Pop 4 (record 4); push 3, 5 from 4.
Heap {3, 5, 5}. Pop 3 (record 3); push 2. Heap {2, 5, 5}. Pop 2 (record 2). Pop 5 (record 5).
Order 1 4 3 2 5, matching the expected output.

brief: Split a binary string into the fewest subsequences so that every subsequence alternates between 0 and 1. Print the count k and the subsequence index of each character.
key_idea: Keep two stacks of subsequence ids: those ending in 0 and those ending in 1. Append each character to a subsequence ending with the opposite bit if one exists; otherwise open a new subsequence.
solution: Maintain endZero and endOne as stacks of subsequence ids.
For character c, if the opposite stack is non-empty, pop its top id and use it; otherwise create a new id k + 1.
Push the used id onto the stack for c (it now ends with c).
Record id for each position; print k and the ids.
Opening a new subsequence only when forced gives the minimum k.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: s = 0011. '0': no endOne, open #1 (endZero = [1]). '0': open #2 (endZero = [1, 2]).
'1': take #2 from endZero, now ends in 1. '1': take #1 from endZero, now ends in 1.
Output k = 2 and ids 1 2 2 1, matching the expected output.

brief: Given an array, remove as few elements as possible so that every remaining value occurs the same number of times (values may vanish entirely). Output the minimum number removed.
key_idea: For a fixed common count C, each value with frequency >= C keeps exactly C copies. Count how many values have frequency >= C for every C and maximize C * (that count).
solution: Count the frequency of each distinct value (sort the array and group equal values).
Let byCount[f] = number of distinct values with frequency f.
Sweep C from n down to 1, maintaining ge = number of values with frequency >= C; track best = max(C * ge).
Answer = n - best.
Checked against brute force over all subsets for 150 small arrays.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test case (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: C = 2: ge = 2, value 4. C = 1: ge = 4, value 4. Best = 4.
Answer = 6 - 4 = 2, matching the expected output.

brief: Given a binary string s and an integer x, find a binary string w of the same length such that s_i = 1 exactly when w has a 1 at position i - x or i + x (where those positions exist). Output w or -1.
key_idea: Every position with s_i = 0 forces w at i - x and i + x to be 0. Start with w all ones, apply these forced zeros, then check that each s_i = 1 still has a 1 partner.
solution: Set w = all '1'.
For each i with s_i = '0', set w[i - x] = '0' (if it exists) and w[i + x] = '0' (if it exists).
For each i with s_i = '1', check that w[i - x] or w[i + x] is '1' (existing positions only).
If any check fails, print -1; otherwise print w. Setting w to 1 wherever allowed maximizes the chance of satisfying the 1s.
Checked against brute force over all w for 150 random cases with n <= 8.
complexity: O(n) time per test case, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: s = 01, x = 1. s_0 = 0 forces w[1] = 0; w starts as 11, becomes 10.
Check s_1 = 1: w[0] = 1, so it holds. Output 10, matching the expected output.
Sample 3: s = 110, x = 1. s_2 = 0 forces w[1] = 0, so w = 101. s_0 = 1 needs w[1] = 1, which fails: output -1.

brief: Tree with n nodes. Give each of the n-1 edges a distinct label from 0..n-2 so that the largest MEX over all node pairs (smallest label missing on the path) is as small as possible. Print the label of each input edge.
key_idea: MEX >= 3 needs labels 0, 1, 2 on one path. If some vertex has degree >= 3, put 0, 1, 2 on three edges at that vertex (no path holds all three), giving max MEX 2. If the tree is a path, every labelling gives n-1, so label along the path.
solution: Compute degrees. If some vertex v has degree >= 3, give its first three incident edges labels 0, 1, 2 and the rest labels 3, 4, ... in any order.
Otherwise the tree is a path: start at a leaf, walk the path, and give the i-th edge label i-1.
Lower bound: any two edges lie on a common path, so max MEX >= 2 for n >= 3; for a path the whole path has all labels, so MEX = n - 1 is forced.
Edge with n = 2 (single edge): path case gives label 0.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, edges 1-2, 1-3. Max degree is 2, so it is a path. Start at leaf 2: edge 1-2 gets 0, then edge 1-3 gets 1.
Output 0 then 1, matching the expected output.
Sample 2: vertex 2 has degree 3 (edges 1-2, 2-4, 2-5), so labels 0, 1, 2 go there; the remaining edges get 3 and 4. Max MEX is 2, which matches the expected answer.

brief: Array of non-zero integers. Insert any integers between adjacent elements so that no contiguous subsegment has sum 0. Output the minimum number of insertions.
key_idea: Track prefix sums within the current segment. When a prefix sum repeats, a zero-sum subarray has appeared; insert one separator there (it resets the sums) and count it.
solution: Keep a set of prefix sums of the current segment, initially {0}, and the running prefix p = 0.
For each element a: p += a. If p is already in the set, count one insertion before a, clear the set to {0}, and set p = a.
Insert p into the set and continue.
Greedy is optimal: cutting as late as possible is never worse, because the first repeat is forced and the cut resets all earlier sums.
Use 64-bit sums (up to 2*10^14).
complexity: O(n log n) time (std::set), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: 1 -5 3 2. Prefix sums 1, -4, -1; then a = 2 gives p = 1, already seen (1 is in the set). Count 1, reset, p = 2.
Output 1, matching the expected output.
Sample 4: 16 -5 -11 -15 10 5 4 -4 gives repeats at -11, 5 and -4 (after each reset), so 3, matching the expected output.

brief: n ice spheres with prices (repeats allowed). A sphere is cheap if its price is strictly less than both neighbours (ends are never cheap). Reorder the spheres to maximize the number of cheap ones; output the maximum and one optimal order.
key_idea: Sort the prices. Put the smallest floor(n/2) values on the even (1-based) positions in ascending order and the rest on the odd positions in ascending order; this construction gives the maximum count of strictly smaller valleys.
solution: Sort the prices ascending.
Let h = floor(n/2). Assign a[0..h-1] to the even 1-based positions 2, 4, ... in order.
Assign a[h..n-1] to the odd 1-based positions 1, 3, 5, ... in order.
Count the valleys c[i] < c[i-1] and c[i] < c[i+1] in the built array and print that count and the array.
Verified against brute force over all permutations for 150 small arrays.
complexity: O(n log n) time (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample: sorted 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 (n=7, h=3). Even positions get 1, 2, 2; odd positions get 3, 4, 4, 5.
Array: 3 1 4 2 4 2 5. Valleys at positions 2, 4, 6: 1 < 3,4; 2 < 4,4; 2 < 4,5.
Count 3 and order 3 1 4 2 4 2 5, matching the expected output.

brief: String of A and B. Replace an adjacent AB with BC or an adjacent BA with CB, earning one coin each time. Find the maximum number of coins.
key_idea: Each B can eat a run of A's adjacent to it, but only in one direction (after eating, a C blocks the other side). Split the string by B's into A-blocks and run a two-state DP over which direction each B eats.
solution: If there is no B, the answer is 0.
Let B positions split the string into blocks b[0..m]: b[0] = A's before the first B, b[m] = A's after the last B, and b[i] = A's between B_i and B_(i+1).
Each B_i either eats right (covers b[i], gain b[i]) or eats left (covers b[i-1], gain b[i-1] unless already covered by B_(i-1) eating right).
DP over B's with state c = whether the previous B ate right: dp1 = max(dp0, dp1) + b[i]; dp0 = max(dp0 + b[i-1], dp1).
Answer = max(dp0, dp1) after the last B. Verified against BFS over all operation sequences on 200 random strings of length up to 8.
complexity: O(|s|) time per test case, O(|s|) space
dry_run: Sample ABA: B at index 1; b[0] = 1, b[1] = 1. Start dp0 = 0, dp1 = -inf.
B_1 eats right: dp1 = 0 + 1 = 1. B_1 eats left: dp0 = 0 + 1 = 1.
Answer max(1, 1) = 1, matching the expected output.
Sample ABBA: blocks 1, 0, 1 with two B's; the DP ends at 2, matching the expected output.

brief: n goods (n even) with weights a_i. Pair them into n/2 packages; a package of total weight w earns floor(w / k). Maximize the total revenue.
key_idea: floor((a+b)/k) = floor(a/k) + floor(b/k) + [a%k + b%k >= k]. The first part is fixed, so maximize the number of pairs whose remainders sum to at least k, found by two pointers on sorted remainders.
solution: base = sum of floor(a_i / k); remainders r_i = a_i % k.
Sort the remainders ascending.
Two pointers l = 0, r = n-1: if r[l] + r[r] >= k, count a pair and move both (l++, r--); otherwise l++ (the smallest remainder cannot pair with the largest, so skip it).
Answer = base + number of pairs.
The greedy pairs as many large-with-small remainders as possible, which is the maximum matching for this threshold condition.
complexity: O(n log n) time per test case (sorting), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: k=3, a = 3 2 7 1 4 8. base = 1+0+2+0+1+2 = 6; remainders sorted: 0 1 1 1 2 2.
(0,2): 2 < 3, skip. (1,2): 3 >= 3, pair 1. (1,2): 3 >= 3, pair 2. Stop when l meets r.
Answer 6 + 2 = 8, matching the expected output.
